canonical_record.label: NIST controlled blocking
canonical_record.summary: NIST describes blocking as holding nuisance factors constant inside homogeneous blocks while varying the factor of interest.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods: 5.3.3.2. Randomized block designs

statement: NIST describes blocking as holding nuisance factors constant inside homogeneous blocks while varying the factor of interest.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.

support.quote:
The basic concept
is to create homogeneous blocks in which the nuisance factors are held
constant and the factor of interest is allowed to vary.

canonical_record.label: NIST balanced blocking criterion
canonical_record.summary: NIST defines a blocking factor by equal occurrence of each primary-factor level at each nuisance-factor level.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods: 5.3.3.2. Randomized block designs

statement: NIST defines a blocking factor by equal occurrence of each primary-factor level at each nuisance-factor level.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Applies to its balanced design description.

support.quote:
A nuisance factor is used as a blocking factor if every level of
the primary factor occurs the same number of times with each level of
the nuisance factor

canonical_record.label: NIST residual nuisance randomization
canonical_record.summary: NIST recommends blocking important nuisance variables and randomizing to reduce contamination by remaining nuisance variables.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods: 5.3.3.2. Randomized block designs

statement: NIST recommends blocking important nuisance variables and randomizing to reduce contamination by remaining nuisance variables.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Recommendation, not a universal measured effect.
scope.quantifiers: A few important factors; remaining factors

support.quote:
Blocking is used to remove the effects of a few of the most important
nuisance variables.  Randomization is then used to reduce the
contaminating effects of the remaining nuisance variables.

canonical_record.label: NIST hypothetical blocked wafer allocation
canonical_record.summary: NIST illustrates a hypothetical design putting four wafers with different dosages in each of three furnace runs.

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods: 5.3.3.2. Randomized block designs

statement: NIST illustrates a hypothetical design putting four wafers with different dosages in each of three furnace runs.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Proposed allocation, not an observed result.

support.quote:
The blocked way to run this
experiment, assuming you can convince manufacturing to let you put four
experimental wafers in a furnace run, would be to put four wafers with
different dosages in each of three furnace runs.  The only randomization
would be choosing which of the three wafers with dosage 1 would go into
furnace run 1, and similarly for the wafers with dosages 2, 3 and 4.

canonical_record.label: Nosek preregistration definition
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. (2018) define analysis preregistration as committing to analytic steps without prior knowledge of outcomes.

statement: Nosek et al. (2018) define analysis preregistration as committing to analytic steps without prior knowledge of outcomes.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.

support.quote: Preregistration of an analysis plan is committing to analytic steps without advance knowledge of the research outcomes.

canonical_record.label: Nosek postdiction diagnosticity warning
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. warn that postdictive NHST analyses may yield p-values of unknown diagnosticity.

statement: Nosek et al. warn that postdictive NHST analyses may yield p-values of unknown diagnosticity.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Methodological warning, not a measured prevalence.

support.quote:
This leaves the observed
P
values with unknown diagnosticity, rendering them uninterpretable. In other words, NHST cannot be used with confidence for postdiction.

canonical_record.label: Nosek 2018 preregistration evidence limit
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. (2018) report theoretical and correlational support for preregistration but insufficient experimental evidence of a reproducibility advantage.

statement: Nosek et al. (2018) report theoretical and correlational support for preregistration but insufficient experimental evidence of a reproducibility advantage.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Time-bound; says nothing about later studies.

support.quote: We say “in principle” because the case for preregistration is theoretically strong as a matter of inductive inference and empirically bolstered by some correlational evidence. However, there is not yet sufficient experimental evidence establishing its superiority for reproducibility.

canonical_record.label: Nosek preexisting-data blinding
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. explain that tests of predictions using preexisting data depend on blinded analysis decisions, which face risks when data have already been observed.

statement: Nosek et al. explain that tests of predictions using preexisting data depend on blinded analysis decisions, which face risks when data have already been observed.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Risk varies with knowledge of prior observations.

support.quote: The extent to which testing predictions is possible on preexisting data depends on whether decisions about the analysis plan are blind to the data.
However, once the data have been observed, there are inevitable risks for blinding.

canonical_record.label: Nosek biased preregistered decision trees
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. warn that preregistered decision trees can still embed bias, such as stopping after achieving p < 0.05.

statement: Nosek et al. warn that preregistered decision trees can still embed bias, such as stopping after achieving p < 0.05.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Hypothetical risk, not observed misuse frequency.

support.quote:
However, it is possible to preregister biases into decision trees. For example, one could preregister testing a sequence of exclusion rules and stopping when one achieves
P
< 0.05. On the positive side, this misbehavior is highly detectable; on the negative side, it invalidates the diagnosticity of statistical inference. Preregistration does not eliminate the possibility of poor statistical practices, but it does make them detectable.

canonical_record.label: Nosek complete reporting across studies
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. argue that reporting all planned outcomes matters because preregistration alone cannot eliminate multiple-comparison and selective-reporting problems.

statement: Nosek et al. argue that reporting all planned outcomes matters because preregistration alone cannot eliminate multiple-comparison and selective-reporting problems.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.

support.quote: Not only is it essential that the analysis plan be defined blind to the research outcomes, all outcomes of that analysis plan must be reported to avoid the problem of selective reporting.

Preregistration does not eliminate the challenge of multiple comparisons or selective reporting across studies, but it does make it possible to effectively correct for multiple comparisons with full reporting.

canonical_record.label: Nosek Registered Reports workflow
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. describe Registered Reports as pre-outcome methodological peer review with in-principle acceptance, followed by review of execution and adherence.

statement: Nosek et al. describe Registered Reports as pre-outcome methodological peer review with in-principle acceptance, followed by review of execution and adherence.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.
scope.uncertainty: Described workflow, not universal journal policy.

support.quote: With Registered Reports, authors submit their research question and methodology to the journal for peer review before observing the outcomes of the research. If reviewers agree that the question is sufficiently important and the methodology to test it is of sufficiently high quality, then the paper is given in-principle acceptance.
At second-stage review, reviewers do not evaluate the perceived importance of the outcomes. Rather, they evaluate the quality of study execution and adherence to the preregistered plan.

canonical_record.label: Nosek exploratory-to-holdout testing
canonical_record.summary: Nosek et al. describe splitting a dataset, sealing the holdout and preregistering exploration-derived predictions before unsealing it.

statement: Nosek et al. describe splitting a dataset, sealing the holdout and preregistering exploration-derived predictions before unsealing it.

scope.assumptions: Source-attributed, not independently established as universal.

support.quote: In a process known as cross-validation, the dataset is split in two.
Sealing a dataset and preregistering the outcomes of the discovery process before unsealing converts postdictions from the initial dataset to predictions for the holdout dataset.
